1_Learning_Objective.Title: 🎯 The "Why Are We Learning This?" (Learning Objective)
1_Learning_Objective.Content: The core takeaway is to help your child recognize the 26 letters of the English alphabet, distinguish between uppercase (capital) and lowercase (small) letters, and understand that letters follow a specific sequence (A to Z). This is the absolute foundation for all reading and writing!

2_The_Hook.Title: 🪝 The Hook (How to start the conversation)
2_The_Hook.Content: While reading their favorite bedtime story, point to the page and casually ask: **'Did you know that every single word in this whole book is made from just 26 special puzzle pieces?'** (Let them guess what those pieces are). Then smile and say: **'They are called letters! Let's meet the alphabet family.'**

Mini_Lessons.What_To_Say: Tell your child: 'There are exactly 26 letters in our alphabet family. Together, they team up to make every word we speak! Let's sing their names from A all the way to Z.'
Mini_Lessons.Home_Example: Sing the ABC song together slowly. Use alphabet blocks, a chart, or write them out and have your child point to each letter as you sing.

Mini_Lessons.Topic: Lesson 2: Big Letters and Small Letters
Mini_Lessons.What_To_Say: Tell your child: 'Every letter has a Big version (Capital) and a Small version (Lowercase). Just like there are grown-ups and kids in a family! The big letters are used to start very special words, like your name.'
Mini_Lessons.Home_Example: Write their name clearly on a piece of paper. Highlight the first capital letter and explain that the rest are small letters because they are following the 'grown-up' leader.

Mini_Lessons.What_To_Say: Tell your child: 'The letters are very polite; they always stand in the exact same line. A is always first, B is second, and Z is always at the very end. We call this the Alphabetical Order.'
Mini_Lessons.Home_Example: Take out just 5 alphabet cards (A, B, C, D, E), mix them up on the floor, and challenge your child to put them back into their 'polite line'.

4_Common_Stumbling_Blocks.Title: 🚧 Common Stumbling Blocks (What to watch out for)
4_Common_Stumbling_Blocks.Content:
At this age, kids often confuse **'b' and 'd'** visually, or think the fast part of the alphabet song **('L-M-N-O-P')** is just one big mashed-up word.
*   **How to clarify:** Slow the song down completely and clap for each individual letter: L, M, N, O, P. For 'b' and 'd', teach them the 'bed' trick: hold up two fists with thumbs pointing up—the left hand makes a 'b' and the right hand makes a 'd'!

Questions.Question: How many letters are there in the whole alphabet family?
When we write your name, do we start it with a big capital letter or a small lowercase letter?
If I am the letter 'C', who is standing in line right in front of me, and who is standing right behind me?
Questions.Expected_Answer: 'B' is in front, and 'D' is behind!

Activities.Name: 1. Letter Detective
Activities.Description: Give your child a magnifying glass (or just have them make 'binoculars' with their hands) and ask them to find 3 things in the living room that start with the letter 'B' or 'C'.

Activities.Name: 2. Playdough Alphabet
Activities.Description: Roll out thin 'snakes' of playdough and help your child bend them to form their favorite letters, focusing on seeing the difference between the uppercase and lowercase shapes.

Activities.Name: 3. The Disappearing Letter Game
Activities.Description: Write A, B, C, D, E on a whiteboard or piece of paper. Tell your child to close their eyes, then erase or cover one letter. Have them open their eyes and guess which letter ran away!
